raw_case_text: We examined a 3-month-old infant with persistent diarrhea and failure to thrive. The male patient was born at term to healthy non-consanguineous Italian parents after an uncomplicated pregnancy. His umbilical separation was delayed. At admission, he had a temperature of 38  C, CRP concentration of 41 mg/L, white blood cell count of 34.6 x 103/mul, polymorphonuclear cell count of 14.11 x 103/mul, lymphocytic cell count of 15.43 x 103/mul, and hypereosinophilia (3.8 x 103/mul). Adenovirus was detected in his stool sample. Physical examination revealed mild dysmorphic features with frontal bossing, micrognathia, hypoplastic nasal wings, and flattened alveolar margins. He presented signs of anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with fine and sparse hair, absent eyebrows, thin translucent skin with dry eczema, and hyperkeratosis (Fig. 1(A)). The absence of sweat glands at skin biopsy confirmed this hypothesis. Radiologic evaluation was performed and the images showed "bone-in-bone appearance" of the femoral, iliac, and ischial bones bilaterally, consistent with a diagnosis of osteopetrosis (Fig. 1(B, B')). His general condition rapidly deteriorated with significant dyspnea, oliguria, and lethargy. He presented acute seizures. A head CT scan was negative. MRI was not performed. He was immediately admitted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit. On admission, he had leukocytosis (52.24 x 103/mul) and the signs of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis with prolonged fever, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia (Hb 6.9 g/dl), elevated ferritinemia (37,300 ng/ml), LDH (2105 U/L), low fibrinogen (93 mg/dl), and hypertriglyceridemia (700 mg/dl). Conventional respiratory and circulatory support with inotropes was necessary. A thoracic scan image was concordant with interstitial pneumonitis. Pneumocystis jirovecii and CMV DNA were identified in the bronchoalveolar lavage by PCR. The patient was successfully treated with meropenem, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, and ganciclovir. The signs of concomitant macrophage activation syndrome were gradually normalized under systemic corticosteroid therapy. During his prolonged hospitalization, the patient also displayed a transient and inconstant lymphedema of the lower limbs. Immunological assay was performed at 4 months of life. The patient presented severe hypogammaglobulinemia with IgG (1.73 g/L with normal range 2.22-8.46 g/L), IgA (0.01 g/L with normal range 0.06-0.6 g/L), and IgM (0.04 g/L with normal range 0.28-0.39 g/L). TRECs and KRECs were normal. Flow cytometry immunophenotyping revealed low NK and B memory cell counts (Table 1). NK cell functional activity (CD107a expression) could not be determined due to the low number of NK cells. Proliferative T cell responses to mitogenic stimuli were normal (Table 1). We performed an analysis of the IKBKG sequence (NM_001099856.3) from both genomic DNA and cDNA and we identified a novel missense mutation c.1238A>G (p.H413R) within exon 10 on the zinc finger domain. The substituted histidine is highly conserved among different species (Fig. 2). Using a bioinformatic system (Polyphen and SIFT-Sort Intolerant From Tolerant), the new mutation is predicted to be damaging with a score of 0.99 (sensitivity 0.09; specificity 0.99) and to affect protein function with a score of 0.00 (intolerant), respectively. The CADD score was also elevated (22.9). We performed a careful dermatological examination of the patient's mother, we did not observe any of the nail, hair, dental, or skin findings typical of incontinentia pigmenti. Moreover, there was no history of dermatological problems in the family. Maternal sequencing on genomic and cDNA revealed the WT IKBKG on both alleles. We evaluated the patient's blood cells after activation with TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and other agonists of TLRs. The response of the patient's blood cells to IL-1beta, LPS (agonist of TLR-4), and SAC was abnormal, in terms of IL-6 production (Fig. 1(C)). Moreover, the response to TNF-alpha was impaired in terms of IL-10 production (Fig. 1(C')). IL-6 and IL-10 production was measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) after 48 h of activation. For persistent bloody diarrhea, hypoproteinemia and feeding intolerance parenteral nutrition was necessary. Colon biopsy showed macroscopic signs of enterocolitis with diffuse eosinophilic infiltrates in the lamina propria of the colon. Despite IV antimicrobial prophylaxis and regular infusions of IV immunoglobulin, at 10 months of age, the patient was readmitted presenting a new episode of catheter-associated bacteremia from E. coli. At 13 months of age, the patient underwent a myeloablative conditioning regimen consisting of thiotepa, treosulfan, and fludarabine followed by haploidentical stem cell transplantation with TCR-alpha/beta and CD19 depletion. He received anti-thymocyte globulin and mycophenolate mofetil with a complete antimicrobial prophylaxis as a prevention of acute GVHD and infectious complications. He died unexpectedly from acute respiratory distress and sepsis due to multiresistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa 6 days post HSCT.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-month-old full-term Italian male infant presented with persistent diarrhea, failure to thrive, fever (38 °C), anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, and osteopetrosis, and rapidly deteriorated into acute dyspnea, oliguria, lethargy, and seizures.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born full-term to healthy non-consanguineous Italian parents after an uncomplicated pregnancy, the infant had delayed umbilical cord separation and presented at 3 months of age with chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and fever (38 °C). Shortly after hospital admission, his condition rapidly deteriorated with severe dyspnea, oliguria, lethargy, acute seizures, and hepatosplenomegaly, prompting urgent transfer to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU).
subjective.past_medical_history: Delayed umbilical cord separation; persistent diarrhea and failure to thrive; born full-term to non-consanguineous Italian parents with no family history of incontinentia pigmenti or immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent (later bloody) diarrhea, failure to thrive, fever, acute dyspnea, oliguria, lethargy, acute seizures, and transient lower limb lymphedema.

objective.physical_examination: Admission temperature 38.0 °C; mild dysmorphic features (frontal bossing, micrognathia, hypoplastic nasal alae, flattened alveolar margins); signs of anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (fine sparse hair, absent eyebrows, thin translucent skin with dry eczema and hyperkeratosis); rapid progression to lethargy, seizures, severe dyspnea, oliguria, hepatosplenomegaly, and transient lower extremity lymphedema.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: WBC 34.6 x 10^3/μL (PMNs 14.11 x 10^3/μL, lymphocytes 15.43 x 10^3/μL, hypereosinophilia 3.8 x 10^3/μL), C-reactive protein (CRP) 41 mg/L, and stool positive for adenovirus. PICU deterioration labs (secondary HLH/MAS): Marked leukocytosis (WBC 52.24 x 10^3/μL), severe anemia (hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL), extreme hyperferritinemia (37,300 ng/mL), elevated LDH (2,105 U/L), hypofibrinogenemia (93 mg/dL), and hypertriglyceridemia (700 mg/dL). Skeletal radiography: Bilateral 'bone-in-bone' appearance of the femoral, iliac, and ischial bones diagnostic of osteopetrosis. Head CT: Negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin and colon biopsies: Skin biopsy confirmed complete absence of eccrine sweat glands; colon biopsy demonstrated eosinophilic enterocolitis with diffuse lamina propria eosinophilic infiltrates. Thoracic scan and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) PCR: Interstitial pneumonitis on thoracic imaging; BAL PCR was positive for both Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA. Immunological and genetic workup (at 4 months): Severe panhypogammaglobulinemia with IgG 1.73 g/L (normal: 2.22–8.46 g/L), IgA 0.01 g/L (0.06–0.6 g/L), and IgM 0.04 g/L (0.28–0.39 g/L); normal TRECs, KRECs, and mitogen T-cell proliferation, but low NK-cell and memory B-cell counts on flow cytometry; impaired blood cell IL-6 response to IL-1beta, LPS, and SAC, and impaired IL-10 response to TNF-alpha on ELISA; genomic/cDNA sequencing of IKBKG (NEMO) identified a de novo hemizygous missense mutation c.1238A>G (p.His413Arg / p.H413R) in exon 10 (zinc finger domain).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: OL-EDA-ID syndrome (osteopetrosis, lymphedema, anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, and immunodeficiency) caused by a novel de novo hemizygous IKBKG (NEMO) zinc-finger mutation (c.1238A>G, p.H413R), complicated at 3 months of age by Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus (CMV) interstitial pneumonia (confirmed by BAL PCR), secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis / macrophage activation syndrome (HLH/MAS), and eosinophilic colitis. Plan and clinical course: Managed in the PICU with mechanical ventilation, inotropic support, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, ganciclovir, meropenem, systemic corticosteroids (which resolved MAS), parenteral nutrition, and regular IVIG replacement. After a catheter-related E. coli bacteremia at 10 months, he underwent TCR-alpha/beta and CD19-depleted haploidentical hematopoietic stem cell transplantation at 13 months (conditioned with thiotepa, treosulfan, fludarabine, ATG, and MMF), but died 6 days post-HSCT from multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa sepsis and acute respiratory distress.
